notes.meaning: Job pauses to give Zophar a turn to speak, but the friends remain silent. Realizing they have given up their arguments, Job resumes his speech with great solemnity. He begins a weighty discourse to give his settled judgment.

Job makes a solemn oath by the living God, which was the strongest pledge an Israelite could offer. Even though he feels God has withheld justice from him and made his life bitter, he still acknowledges God's supreme authority. He brings his honest pain before the very Lord he swears by.

Job reminds his listeners that God gave him the breath of life in the beginning. As long as that divine gift keeps him alive and conscious, his mind remains clear to testify to the truth. His physical suffering has not clouded his ability to know right from wrong.

Job declares the terms of his solemn vow. He promises that he will not speak falsehood or utter anything deceitful. Falsely confessing to terrible sins just to satisfy his friends would be a wicked lie, and he refuses to do it.

Job flatly refuses to agree that his friends are correct in their harsh charges against him. Conceding that he is a secret villain would betray the truth. He resolves to hold on to his sincere devotion to God until his dying day.

Job clings firmly to his upright life and will not let anyone take it away. When he looks back over his past, his conscience does not convict him of leading a double life. A clear conscience gives him courage even in deep suffering.

Job expresses how deeply he despises genuine evil. He would rather his worst enemies face the dreadful end of the wicked than ever choose wicked ways himself. He wants no part in the dishonest life his accusers imagine he has lived.

Job asks what good earthly profits do for a godless person when life comes to an end. A hypocrite might gain wealth and status in this world, but those things are useless when God requires the soul. Earthly success cannot buy eternal peace.

When sudden disaster falls, God will not answer the desperate cries of someone who lived a lie. A person who ignored God all along has no claim on his favor in the day of trouble. Job points out that insincere faith leaves a person helpless in crisis.

A godless person finds no true joy in God and only prays when he wants something selfish. He quickly stops seeking God when hard times come or answers are delayed. In contrast, Job continues to reach out to God even amid unbearable loss.

Job offers to teach his friends how God's sovereign power and providence truly work. Relying on divine help, he will not hide the real principles behind God's dealings with humanity. He wants to clear away their mistaken notions about suffering.

Job appeals to what the friends have witnessed in real life. They have seen that the wicked often prosper for a time while good people suffer. He asks why they continue with such empty, useless arguments that contradict basic human experience.

Job outlines what ultimately awaits the cruel oppressor and the wicked person from the Almighty. While evil people may flourish for a season, judgment will eventually catch up with them. God will ensure that justice is done in the end.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern commentators suggest that verses 13 to 23 originally formed the missing third speech of Zophar, because its description of the wicked man's doom closely mirrors Zophar's earlier words.

notes.meaning: Even if a tyrant has a large family, which was regarded as a sign of blessing, his children will face ruin. Many will die by war or violence, and those who survive will suffer from severe hunger. Their father's ill-gotten wealth cannot secure their future.

Those in the tyrant's household who survive war and famine will be swept away by deadly disease. Their burials will be hurried and obscure, without honor. Even their widows will not mourn, having lived under bitter oppression themselves.

The wicked man may pile up massive quantities of silver as easily as dust. He may also fill his storerooms with costly garments as plentiful as clay. Yet accumulating vast riches cannot protect his heart or his life.

Though the ungodly man stockpiles fine clothing, upright people will end up wearing it. Innocent individuals will divide up his hoard of silver. God's providence ultimately redirects wealth so that it serves those who love what is right.

The estate built by the wicked man is as fragile as a moth's cocoon. It is like the temporary shelter a watchman sets up in a vineyard for the harvest season. It looks protective for a moment, but it is soon blown away and dismantled.

The rich man lies down in wealth, but his fortune and life end abruptly. In the blink of an eye, or when he wakes, his possessions are gone and he is swept away. Death strips away all outward power in an instant.

Overwhelming terrors rush upon the ungodly man like an unstoppable flood. In the middle of the night, God's sudden judgment carries him away like a fierce storm. He finds no shelter from the dread that overtakes his conscience.

A scorching, violent east wind picks up the wicked man and whisks him out of his place. The majestic estate where he thought he would live forever cannot hold him. He is driven away from everything he labored to build.

The fierce storm of judgment pummels the wicked man without showing any pity. He runs as fast as he can to get away from its fury, but there is nowhere left to hide. Those who refuse to seek God's grace cannot escape his justice.

The storm drives the ruined oppressor from the scene while onlookers clap their hands and hiss in disgust. They celebrate that a cruel tyrant has finally been removed from power. His downfall leaves behind only disgrace and contempt.
